utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, ma'am. The accused are all here. I see Mr. Josse isolated today, on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Your Honour, is going to be here later. He's gone to the Serbian embassy to try to sort out our client's provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. The rest, I see, are all here. The rest are all here. Okay. Prosecution is Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. McCloskey. And I think we can safely start. The witness is already in the courtroom. I just wanted to check with you, Madam Registrar, that he's got facial distortion and pseudonym only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all. All right. And his number will be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence as a Prosecution witness. Our rules require that before you do so, you enter a -- make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Registrar is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration. Please stand up. Read that solemn declaration aloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. You may have been -- you may have followed what I said earlier, that Prosecution sought on your behalf two protective measures. Namely, your name will not be used, we will use a pseudonym; and no one will be able to see your face outside these four walls. You have, I suppose, been informed about these protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I just wanted to have confirmation from you that you are satisfied with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. First that will be Mr. Vanderpuye who obviously you will have met already who will examine you in chief and he will then be followed by the various Defence teams in cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, counsel. At this time I'd like the pseudonym sheet please presented to the witness. It's P02318. Please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the document in front of you, and without telling us what it says can you confirm that you are the person named in it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would counsel like to have a look at the document, if necessary? May I inquire, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. That document will go straight under seal and will be preserved in that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall giving testimony -- giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you signed on the 18th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement that you gave at that time truthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity prior to today to read your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you read the statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, in my native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the language in which you originally gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what language is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It's Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the statement you read was correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the statement, as you read it, fairly and accurately reflect your declaration or what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the statement fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time I would offer the statement into evidence. It is P02317 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. And obviously that also will go under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have also a very brief 92 ter summary that I would like to read into the record with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to draw your attention to your work with the radio relay unit in the army after July 1995, or from July 1995 forward. Now, with respect to that work, can you tell us briefly what procedures, if any, you followed with relation to recording intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: When you're taping intercepted conversations or communications, there was a standard procedure. At a certain frequency, a given frequency, which would be provided in an order, we would scan specific channels, 24 channels. The channels where we picked up some activity would then be monitored. From the point in time when an activity was picked up at a certain channel, when the scanning stopped, that was the moment when the tape recorder was turned on. They were mostly UHER tape recorders. That's when you would depress the pause, when the conversation began. If the conversation was interesting, if there was any information there that was useful to us, for the purposes of defence, those conversations would be adequately conveyed or transferred to the operations work book which was in front of us on the desk. Then the work book, depending on the type of the conversation or its urgency, would be used by another man to retype the conversation and then it would be sent to the corps command through a Paket connection. If the conversation was not that important, during the day, then all the conversations would be retyped and sent to the corps command. That was the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the procedure that was followed by you at the location at which you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that a procedure that was communicated to you by your superiors for you to follow in the facility in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it was a standard protocol that was followed by the intercept operators in the facility in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: That should have been the standard protocol. I can only talk about the standard protocol during the shifts when I was on duty. The shifts that I was on duty or that my people covered, that was the standard protocol in such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review a packet of ten intercepts that I presented you with in my office sometime ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular, did you review the handwritten material that was contained in the packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that handwriting yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you recognise in addition to the handwriting any signature or mark at the end of the handwritten material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: At the end of each of the handwritten document was my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the originals of the handwritten material that you were presented with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to compare the originals to the photocopies that are contained within the packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you satisfy yourself that the photocopies conformed to the original versions of that handwritten material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: The photocopies absolutely conform to the original versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the handwritten material, was that material that you prepared during the course and scope of your job at the facility in which you worked back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do the -- does the handwritten material [Microphone not activated] was the handwritten [French translation coming over English channel]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the interpreters are trying to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the microphone was not on the right channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- please Mr. Bourgon and Madam Fauveau. Is it okay now? Yes, go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you could repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the handwritten material -- was it prepared close in time to the events that are recorded in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: They were prepared very shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not going to have you look at all the intercepts that you reviewed but I would like to draw your attention to a couple of them, if I may, the first of which is in tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll just orient the Court. Tab 6 is P01133 and in particular I'm referring to the handwritten notebook entry 1133 C, if I could have that just displayed for a moment to the witness. I'm just going to have the English translation also put up on the screen for the benefit of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the top of the left document? Just have a read of that and let me know when you're finished with that, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Will you please clarify what this pertains to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Talking about the very first recording on your left side, should be on the screen, I was just asking you to refer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just note that the translation that is up on the screen is a translation not of the document that is on the left side. According to what's on the screen, the translation is of the document 7820 and not 4841. If we could have the right translation with the right document it would be -- then we can better compare the two. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Although I cannot read, of course, the text or the handwriting on the left-hand side of the monitor, I do, however, see that there is no part of that document which, on three subsequent lines indicate the initials capital C:, X:, C: in that sequence. So there is probably a problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But where is the X?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think my esteemed counsel is correct. I think what we are looking at here is a translation of the printout version of the handwritten intercept. And for that reason I guess I won't offer this translation as a translation of what's in the text. It's really kind of to assist us through it. But I could have the witness simply just read the written material into the record, if that would satisfy counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that would be extremely helpful. Mr. Bourgon? I think we can proceed in that manner. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would, Witness, if you can see that well enough, hopefully, could you read the first intercepted communication that's indicated in the page on your left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: "They didn't call here. You take the message. Question: Which? Answer: They are looking for Jankovic and Popovic. Say that Jankovic escorted these people to Kladanj and Popovic went with APCs towards Konjevic Polje."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall having transcribed this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall in substance what this communication relates to or why it's important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: As one can see from this conversation, every little piece of information was important for us. There is quite a lot of information in this conversation. They were looking for Jankovic and Popovic. Jankovic had escorted people to Kladanj and Popovic had gone with APCs towards Konjevic Polje. At that time those were very important pieces of information for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us why, if you can recall, why that information was so important to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It was important because it had to do with the problems in Srebrenica. Any information was important to us. Let me tell you once again, in this conversation, they mention specific names and specific needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'd like to refer your attention to a different intercept, if I could. That's behind tab number 10. And the reference number is P01149. I'd like to have 1149C, please, displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand I have the same problem with this translation as well, so I'll have the witness, if he could, read the text of the handwritten material into the record as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can move along the same lines as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The idea, when I say let's proceed the same way we did before, is point the excerpt or the part that you are interested in to the witness and ask him to read it out aloud as he did in the previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, unless there is a challenge on the part of the Defence whether this is a correct translation we can move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I don't see that there is one, so we'll proceed, I guess, along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review this particular intercept, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall having transcribed this particular intercept as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us why it was that you recorded this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't think it needs to be explained. Whoever reads this intercept will fully understand why it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, just for the purposes of the record, could you tell us why it is that you recorded it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Of course I can. In this intercept -- just a minute, yes. Let me take a closer look at it. In this intercept, they specifically mention -- or, rather, indirectly mention the President of Republika Srpska, Karadzic, and that alone makes it a very interesting intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the intercept itself, you have a designation that's in quotes referring to something that the president says and that is that all the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow. And that's specifically in quotes. Can you tell us why that's the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It's in quotation marks because they quote the specific words of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, placing things in quotation marks, is that something that you would normally do in order to attribute a given statement to a person that's speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't understand the essence of your question. Only the quotation refers to specific words uttered by a person. Only that part was put in quotation marks, as is the case here. This is a conversation that President Karadzic had over an intermediary. These words: "All the goods must be placed inside the warehouse before 12.00 tomorrow." These words are in quotation marks precisely because these are the words of President Karadzic. And apparently they are saying to him: "Deronjic, this is what the president says," and then they give the words uttered by him, and that's precisely why these words are in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Just bear with me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have nothing further at this time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Have you decided about the roster that you are going to adopt? Mr. Zivanovic, who is appearing for Colonel Popovic will go first. How long do you expect your cross-examination to last, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think it will take me more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please put on the screen Exhibit 1133, introduced by the Prosecution, together with the translation, which is tab 6?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1133 A, B, C? Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. 00801481 -- actually, A and B. Could you please scroll down a little bit? And could you simultaneously put up B on the screen? Or even better, would you please show B? I actually don't know if this is B or C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we need to know, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're fully right, Your Honour. I apologise. Instead of the right-hand version, could we see the handwritten version? Could we see the handwritten one, please? All right. That's fine. Thank you. This is the version we saw earlier. Could we see together with what we saw when the Prosecutor was questioning the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. McCloskey draw my attention to the fact that the prior -- well, what was displayed on the screen previously had certain initials, and I wasn't aware of whether or not it was being broadcast at this time but if it's not, then fine. If so, then maybe there is something we can do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was not broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, but I have a confirmation that it was not broadcast. Let's somebody verify it for sure to make sure. It's okay. All right. So then provided we keep on using the same system, not broadcasting documents unless you are specifically authorised to, I think we can proceed with safety. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in the English version, we see that the frequency indicated is 785.000 megahertz. We can't see that in your original notebook. So can you explain that for us, the reason to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes. Very easily. This is the frequency of the main wave. When we receive an order, we receive it with a frequency and with a certain direction. That means that this is the frequency to which we adjust our radio sets and the direction to which we turn our antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. I am not asking you about the frequency. I'm just saying that it is not indicated in the original notebook and can you please explain how come it is written in the typewritten text but it is missing in the original notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: In the notebook, in certain intercepts, in certain conversations, the frequency is not indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, who entered this frequency? Was it the typist from crypto protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I had absolutely no contact with the typist in crypto protection department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are overlapping. You need to slow down a little bit. And, sir, when Mr. Zivanovic finishes his question, do not bump straight into with your answer. Allow a very short interval of time, because what is being said by both of you, who speak the same language, is being translated to us. We don't know your language. We don't understand it, so it has to be translated into English and into French. And if you overlap, the -- some of the words will be missed by the interpreters. So a brief pause between question and answer, please. All right, Mr. Zivanovic, and witness. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the original and give us the time of the intercept that you discussed with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I can't see the beginning of the original version. Since this is a copy, I can't see it. I see only minutes. But judging by the conversation below, which was at 10.37, I would say that the previous one was at 10.27.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then agree that the time in translation is 10.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But if you look at the opposite side it says 10.30; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the signature at the bottom of this conversation from the copy in this notebook. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are these your initials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning and the end of my last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, the interpreters haven't heard the witness's answer and that's because, still, you haven't heeded what I've said and you are still overlapping. The question was, first, there was one question, are these your initials; and you said yes, and the end of my last name. And then Mr. Zivanovic proceeded with another question, and we should redact line 13, which was excuse me, and he referred you to your second letter. Let's go into private session now for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, while we were in private session, Mr. Zivanovic for accused Popovic concluded his cross-examination. And we have now -- we are now starting with the cross-examination of Mr. Ostojic, lead counsel for Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. How are you? Sir, I want to follow up on a couple of questions that you just described for us here. You say mostly -- on page 22, lines 7 through 9, just recently. "Mostly we had two work posts or two stations." Can you be a little bit more precise for me, sir, and identify when in fact you had two work posts or work stations and when it increased or decreased? And specifically if you can concentrate on the period of June through August 1995 for me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that specifically. A lot of time has passed since then. I don't remember. So I'm talking about what the equipment was on the desk and when they were activated. I cannot tell you what they were. In any case, one RRU1 and one RRU800 were used. I don't know if at specific times both of them were used simultaneously. That's something that I cannot tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anyway, my question wasn't clear enough. What I'm asking you, sir, was there any time during the period of 1995 when you had more than two work posts or two work stations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact date. A lot of time has passed since then. I cannot be certain about something that I'm not sure about. I'm not sure when this work station was used, which month. It was used as needed. It depended on the amount of the activity and if the work station was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, can you direct me to someone who would know, sir? Do you know any individual who today would know exactly how many work stations you had in June through August of 1995 at that site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: This is something that the platoon commander would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about, sir, with respect to notebooks? On page 12, line 12, you say in answer to my learned colleague's question, that you "had mostly one notebook." Can you be more precise and tell me in June through August of 1995 if you had at that time one or more notebooks at the site where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: One notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you a little bit about the frequency. You state on page 18, lines 21 through 23: "When we receive an order, we receive it with a frequency of the main wave." My question to you, sir, is: Did you ever scan the receiver or mixer to find a frequency on your own or did you strictly comply with the orders given to you and listen to only the frequency that you were directed to listen to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: My assignment as squad commander, amongst other things, was to scan frequencies from time to time because of some new radio relay nodes, and because of something like that, we would not leave one post for another. For example, the other work station was something that I often used during the night to scan frequencies, not channels but frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 10 today, lines had through 7 you told us: "If the conversation was interesting, if there was any information that -- there that was useful to us," you would record it; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought he said something different, Your Honour, but I'll ask him again. No or yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I heard you. The transcript reflected different answer, sir, so I'm sorry, that's why I asked you again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Perhaps there was a misunderstanding, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please don't apologise. Thank you. Now, sir, can you tell me what training you have to determine what information that you were intercepting would be deemed relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm objecting to the question because it is kind of unintelligible as it's written in the transcript, and I don't know what my learned colleague means by deemed relevant, by whom and I don't understand that question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has, throughout the examination-in-chief [inaudible] questions from Mr. Zivanovic, explained why certain excerpts were selected precisely because he said they were of interest. And what is being -- he's being asked now is to explain whether he had any training, obviously previously or at any time, which enabled him select one excerpt from another, for relevance and importance purposes. This is how I understand the question by Mr. Ostojic. He will correct me if I'm wrong, and I think it's a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did I understand your question, well, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Most definitely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you perhaps can repeat it. If you could kindly repeat it. I think the witness has understood exactly what it is. If he can answer it, he can answer it straight away. If he needs the question to be repeated, then we'll have it repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what training did you have to determine what information you were intercepting would be deemed relevant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific training, but in the war situation, for us, any information was important because we were not just working from the station where I was working at. There were several different locations where other groups were working. So we could put together a mosaic from different kinds of information. So if I felt that some information was worth something, I would record it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it was on an individual intercept operator basis, if that individual felt it was important, they would record it; if that individual felt that it was not important, they wouldn't record it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: All information was record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now when you say "recorded," just so that we can understand each other better, you're saying that it was recorded in the handwritten notebook; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. Everything that was intercepted at specific channels, there was a standard procedure. There was a habit formed, you would depress the pause on the tape recorder. Everything that we listened to would be recorded. However, a lot of that was not of interest, so that was not then transcribed into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about those procedures, if you will, for a moment or two. You stated in at least the summary that was read to us, that there was an established protocol. Can you tell us if that was a written protocol or an oral protocol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It was an oral protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the protocol, sir, also discuss various shorthand descriptions that you would make in your notebooks, such as quotation marks or dots or dashes or identity of individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I have to go back to the previous question, I'm sorry. The protocol, as far as I was concerned, was an oral protocol. I don't know if my platoon commander had a written order. However, the order and the instructions were conveyed to me verbally, just like everything else about brackets, dashes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, share with us to the best of your recollection what the rest of those protocols or procedures were, such as brackets or dashes. What did they instruct you to do when you were maintaining these notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't understand what sentence was I -- how I was supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll explain the question, maybe break it down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did your platoon commander instruct you as to how to use certain abbreviations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: My platoon commander did not say anything about certain abbreviations but about certain marks such as the question mark, three dashes, parentheses, everything that is not heard that you're not sure of. In that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. And those are the specific protocols I wanted to discuss with you. Share with us to the best of your recollection what it is that you were instructed with respect to all the "established protocols."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I cannot define your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... break it down. Did your platoon commander or anyone instruct you as to when you should put quotation marks on any of the intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. That is something that you would already know based on what you know of grammar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the platoon commander or anyone, sir, instruct you as to how to identify, if you could not hear a second party to a purported conversation, how would you designate that? Did he instruct you on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: This was discussed, but nothing was specific. It depends on the group that was noting it. Somebody would use one, two; somebody would use X and Y to indicate unidentified speakers. Somebody wouldn't use anything except for a dash.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What, if any, instructions were you given relating to conversations that you were unable to hear? What would be the designation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: A whole conversation or a part of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll take both. Tell me what the protocol was for the entire conversation and then tell me what the protocol was for a part of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: A conversation that could not be heard wouldn't be in there, but a part of a conversation that was inaudible but that was part of a whole would have an explanation or there would be written in brackets that the next part of the conversation could not be heard, if it was just a small part of the conversation, a word or two or three words, you would make a few longer dashes there. If something was unclear, if we were not sure about a word but we sort of guessed that that was it but we were not 100 per cent sure, we would put a question mark in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, these question marks, sir, is it fair that they mean and denote that an assumption is made in the context of the transcription where there is some uncertainty; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Just pertaining to a specific word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your platoon commander, sir, ever tell you that it would be acceptable to go back in the notebook and to add a letter or to change something in an intercepted conversation? Did he ever tell you that's acceptable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it, sir, be acceptable to do that, to change or alter the purported participant in a conversation after you had initially made that recordation in a notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Not in my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you think, sir, that the other shifts had different rules or established protocols that they followed? Different from your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: If you're asking for my opinion, I think that the rules were the same, but I can speak only about my shift because that's when I was there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to direct your attention to tab 8 [sic] that my learned colleague from the Prosecutor discussed with you earlier this morning. And that's the conversation that I think you told us you deemed that it was important, and I think because you said it was the President of Republika Srpska. Just directing your attention to that. And with the Court's permission, if we could have that document and the ELMO. Tab 10. I thought I said tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the transcript we had 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, tab 10. You only used two, 3 and 10 so I thought I had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. We've got it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can have that upon the ELMO, please. If I can also have the English version which has the ERN ending 2586 next to it, please. Doesn't look like the English version but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to focus your attention on that quote that you made with the quotation marks. You say: "All the goods must be placed inside the warehouses between 12 noon." And then I want you to tell us, sir, because in that statement you said that that was something that the intermediary, I think as you put it, relayed specifically the quotes from the president. But if you go - scroll up a little bit, or if you do, sir, about five lines, it has another colon. And then it says: "Deronjic: The president is asking how many thousands?" Do you see that? And if you can just reconcile for me, sir, why you don't have quotes around that but you do on the lower one, just so I can better understand this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I can explain. This part of the conversation at the top did not seem to be a direct quotation to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell me what classification you have as an amateur radio operator? Is it C, B or A? What certification, not classification.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Class B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I noticed in this tab 10 document that we are looking at that you as an experienced and qualified intercept operator in July of 1995 intercepted a conversation where a speaker uses or cites numbers such as thousands, or in fact 2 was used several times. And I note in the B/C/S version, as we call it, that you had written out the number 2 or the number thousands by spelling it out as opposed to using the numerical number. Am I correct, sir, that that was a protocol that was established in order to develop accuracy, specificity and clarity? Is that why you did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. That was just a habit of mine, simply, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair, sir, to state that by writing the number out as opposed to using numbers, that it does indeed make it more accurate, clear and specific as to what the purported participant in a conversation may or may not have said? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It's possible, even though I wasn't thinking about that at the time but just about what I was listening to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you would have written a number like a thousand, 1000, would you put a comma after the 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I just wouldn't. I don't know why but I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you put a dot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Maybe I would put a dot but maybe I wouldn't. I think it's just a question of habit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Sir, let me ask you this: If someone in an intercepted conversation would have asked you as an experienced and qualified intercept operator and you overheard a conversation and he said, "3 to 500" how would you record that? How would you write it in the book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It depends on the situation where -- let's just clarify whether we are talking about that time or now. The times are different. Now a person is more at ease. At that time a person was quite stressed. There was a lot of conversations. There was a lot of work. So you do not pay attention to many things. What is important is to transfer to the paper what is transcribed from the tape recorder, what was recorded. So you can look and see here, not just in my case, that not much attention was paid to grammatical mistakes because of the speed and because many other things dictated by the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Don't misunderstand me, sir, I'm not criticising that you wrote it out alphabetically. I'm just asking you, sir, given the fact that it was quite stressed and there were a lot of conversations, am I correct, then, that there could have been many mistakes that were made in writing down the purported conversations that you were intercepting. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. He's answered it. But Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just object to the question because it really calls for speculation and something that's clearly outside this witness's ken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we fully agree with you. Unfortunately, he had already answered and no damage done because he said no in any case. So ... Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you still haven't answered my other question. I know you're now at ease, and it's not the -- obviously and thankfully not the same stressful situation where you were listening to many conversations. But how would you record a conversation if a person said, "3 to 500." How would you record that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Depends on the situation. Perhaps I would put it down in letters, three to five hundred, maybe I would just use numbers, maybe I would put -- spell it out. It depends on the circumstances, on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just into private session for a couple more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Ostojic. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, we have a break in five minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe it's better to wait until after the break, but as the Trial Chamber sees fit I'm ready to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We'll do what you feel is more convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then I prefer to wait until after the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is an area you can cover in five minutes, then we can go on for the next five minutes. If not then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we have a 30-minute break starting from now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a few questions for you this morning, and I would begin by asking you some clarification with respect to something that you mentioned in your statement. If need be, I will -- I can show you your statement. But you explained that in each squad, and you being the commander of one of those squads, there were five to six members. Can you provide us a bit more information as to how exactly it worked over a 24-hour period, how were those five to six members used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Depending on the number of members within a squad, if there were no fixed business hours, then we would create the schedule depending on how tired people were, what their mood was. We would split the entire day, the 24 hours of the day, so that all of the hours were covered. I think we would split it in six hour segments, depending on the activities. But mostly six hour segments when there were no numerous activities, and if there were a lot of activities, then two people would work together. And there were no fixed business hours. They would work until there was work. So we would take turns, some people would go and rest and sleep, which was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that for any period of five to six hours, then there would be one person that would be on duty? That would be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: One to two, because we had two devices, RRU1 and RRU800. In the third shift, during the night, there would always be one person on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'm just trying to picture how the section worked. Now, you mention in your statement that sometimes you knew the name of the participant and then that you would write it down. My understanding is that that is when the name of the person was mentioned in the conversation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if a person used a false name or a wrong name in a conversation, you would still write the name that you would hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also mentioned that -- and I tried to quote your words, "If I recognised the participant's voice, I would write it down." Now, I just want, like to you clarify. When you say "recognise the voice of the participant," that is because you heard the voice before? Is that how you recognise those voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Quite naturally, I heard the voice. For example, let me explain. If my wife were to call me on the telephone, she doesn't need to introduce herself. I will know that that's her. So the voices that you hear frequently, you recognise without a problem. That's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me clarify my question. If you're -- because you used the exact example you just used, if your wife calls you, the first time she calls you, you will recognise her voice. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if it's a person that you don't know, it will take a few times before you recognise the voice? If you can answer just for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: The first time, when you hear a voice, you cannot recognise it. But as you listen to that voice for a period of time, for example, if you listen to that voice for an entire day, let alone for 22 or 23 months, then quite naturally you recognise that voice without a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that's what the purpose of my question, is that when you say when "I recognised the voice," that recognition was based on hearing that voice over and over again, and not on the fact that you knew the person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also said in your statement that it was always necessary to listen to a conversation several times. And just, if I go back to an answer you also mentioned to my colleague the fact that there was lots of stress and the fact that you had to listen to a conversation many times, that was because it was not easy to fully grasp what those conversations, the way they were recorded on that tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: All of that depended on how it was recorded, depending on the quality of the recording. In some cases, there was no need to listen over and over again because the conversation was clear. And if there were any dilemmas, whether what we heard was accurate or not, or whether something was said quietly, then we would listen very carefully. Sometimes one of the colleagues who were not present at work would be called in to help, so that what was recorded in the notebook would be fully accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I understand from when you had this meeting with my colleague from the Prosecution, would I be correct in saying that sometimes you had to listen to the tape as many as 20 times in order to transcribe the conversation correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how many times, but sometimes it would be very many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you called in a colleague who was not on shift to listen to a tape to help you out, then after hearing both of you that tape carefully, you would come to some kind of an agreement an as to what that tape said. Would that be the normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when this procedure took place that you had to call somebody else to give you some assistance, that was not indicated anywhere in the transcript, whether it was one that you could listen the first time, one that you could listen or transcribe after 20 times or one which you required some help, that's not written on any of the -- of in your notes in the notebook, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when after seeking the assistance of someone who was not on shift or someone who was on shift, you were still not sure, then you indicated in your statement that there was many ways that you could indicate the fact that you could not hear what was on the tape. One of those ways, and we'll go through the list of them, one of those ways was you would put a question mark if it's a specific word that you could not make out. Was that one of the ways?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: A question mark would be placed only if we wrote a word but were not fully certain of it. Only then would we place a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then, if you could not hear a person at all, sometimes you would use -- you put dots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was there any kind of a protocol concerning the number of dots, in terms of the duration of the sentence or of the segment that you could not hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: We would put dots -- rather, there was no protocol. There was no standard procedure, but based on the procedure that we were used to, we would put dots only if we could not understand one to three words. If there was a longer segment that was not audible, then we would write in parentheses that that segment was not audible and then we would continue transcribing what we could hear after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I also understand that in some cases, you simply left a blank. Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. What do you mean by "blank"? We would always mark it in some way. We would either put dots or we would put in parentheses that a certain section was not properly recorded or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, having reviewed the intercepts that were presented to us by the Prosecution, in some cases there are three dots, in some cases there are more dots. And I'm talking about your own intercepts. Was there a difference between three dots or five dots? Did that make a difference to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: The number of dots is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So then it would be at least three words but could be more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. We would do it only if one to three words were not audible, at least based on my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just one last question in respect of this procedure: You answered to a question of one of my colleagues that you thought that this was a standard procedure but you could only tell for the people that were on your shift. Now, I'd just like to know, did you ever verify what was going on and how the others did the work or you simply gave the instructions? I'll try to make my question more precise. Was there a second verification with the notes produced by your colleagues on your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no second verification. All of us there were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the intercept that was at tab number 6, and I'll put the number. Tab number 6 would be Prosecution Exhibit 1105 -- sorry, 1133. And I'd like to put on the e-court, if I could, Exhibits C and B together, one side by side. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can it be done?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be in a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this was -- I would just like to direct your attention, if I look at the one on the right, it is the conversation that was intercepted at 10.30, and I compare that with -- on the left, a conversation at 10.30 is the first one on top and that is where you see the number 4841. Now, I note from comparing these two that the first one does not have the X, the first one being your handwritten one. It does not have the X to indicate the person that is speaking. It does not have the direction, and it does not have the frequency. Now, this was covered already by my colleague, I'll just add another question on to that difference, because you mentioned that you had no access to the typist, and that was this morning on page 19, lines 4 to 9. So I take it that given this difference and given the fact that you had no access to the typist, my understanding would be, and I suggest to you, that the typist had something more than your notes, than the notebook, to produce the typewritten version. He must have had something else in order to make it more complete. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It seems that you didn't quite understand me when I said previously, what I said. I did not have insight into his work. We cooperated, but he was a member of another squad and he did his work. Retyping the handwritten material was what he did and I was absolutely not interested in his work. We received frequencies in orders, and we would work on a frequency until we received a new order. So, for example, we would work on one frequency for as long as a month. So that in our version of documents, in handwritten documents, we would only indicate the frequency in the beginning and you can see it based on our documents, and following that we would only be interested in channels because we already knew the frequency. The frequency would be changed by way of orders so when a new order would come we would change frequency and sometimes we would work on one frequency for 15 days, 20 days or a month. As for the difference in time, it is there because the recording was taken off the tape at 10.27 and that means that within three minutes it was retyped and forwarded. Based on that you can conclude yourself that it was one of the very important intercepts, at least from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, looking at your statement, you mention in your statement that: "When I began recording the conversation," now I quote from the statement, "I would note the time, frequency and channel on a separate piece of paper." Was that separate piece of paper given to the typist or did you keep it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. This piece of paper was not given to us. It was just there to assist us. Since we would transcribe 2, 3, 4 intercepts simultaneously -- or, rather, I apologise, we would record these conversations simultaneously, and we could not record them in the notebook, so all of us would have a piece of paper where we would note something down, or, rather, we would note the timer on the tape recorder. For example, we would say conversation number 1, the following participants, from this number to this number, and then the next conversation from this number to that number. So this piece of paper was important to us only until we transcribe the intercepts and recorded them in the notebook. Following that it wasn't important at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that piece of paper was then discarded or burned or whatever? But it was not given to the typist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier this morning that you would always sign the intercepts after -- you put your signatures at the end of each intercept. Now, I'd like to display on the e-court Exhibit 1102 Bravo. And my question is simply: If an exhibit does not have your signature, would that mean that it wasn't written by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: In this portion that I can see, the intercept was not signed. This is the intercept that I transcribed. This is my handwriting. Now, as to why it wasn't signed, I can't tell you right now. Perhaps I did this in haste. Perhaps I forgot to sign it. I really have no explanation for this. All I can do is confirm that this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the fact that you did not sign it, as you mention, could be because of haste or the stressful situation or because you were doing more than one thing at the same time, and it would be normal in such a stressful situation that sometimes you can forget a word or two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. That wasn't normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a look at tab number 5, and that is Exhibit 1105, and if we can put on the ELMO 1105 Alpha and 1105 Charlie. I said the ELMO, I'm sorry, I meant e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We can have one on the ELMO and one in e-court since we have two different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Like we did last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's not possible to put them side by side on the e-court, the A and the C, so if we can put maybe the Alpha on the e-court and then the C, or Charlie, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, these are two versions of the same -- of the same intercept and both of them are in English, so I will read the one that is on the ELMO for you so that you can understand in your language. It reads as follows. First it says the participants are X and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. And then the text of the intercept is: "Conversation between unidentified participant X and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. X told him that he has only two buses. He can requisition some without papers and an order. They have problems with fuel. They don't have enough." My first question, sir, is this appears to be -- to me to be a summary of a conversation and not what the people said. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: This is the typed version, so I cannot really talk about that. This is not my part. I would like to talk about only those intercepts that are in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then let's display 1105 Bravo, which is the handwritten version. Okay. So on the -- you have the version that I just read to you, and then you have beside the one that is handwritten. My first question is simply that the handwritten version, this appears to me that you are not quoting verbatim what was heard on the tape but that this is more a description of a conversation. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I agree, in principle. This is just a summary. A part of the conversation that lasted, I don't know how long, I can't really say, but this is the interesting part, a small part of it was interesting. There was no need to literally transcribe everything. There is just a brief summary indicating specific details. The rest of the conversation did not contain important information, as far as we are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now maybe you can help me out because the two translations that I have are not identical, and maybe you can tell me which one corresponds to your handwritten version because in the first one it appears we have one participant X and in the second it appears that we have "they," as being more than one person. Which one corresponds to your handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: The version without the participants is in my handwriting. This is the part that was summarised. So you can see that there are no specific participants but the other intercepts indicate how the collocutors were marked. In the summaries, this isn't there. But again I repeat I can only speak about the handwritten intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second thing I'd like to draw your attention to with respect to your handwritten version is the fact that it would appear to say that "they," whoever the participants are, cannot requisition buses without having the proper papers. Is that what your handwritten version says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: My version literally says: "Some cannot be requisitioned without the papers, without the orders, they are having problems with fuel." So some cannot be requisitioned without an order. Not all, just some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I won't ask you that question but I will simply draw the attention of the Court to the fact that on the other document that we have, which is a translation of the typed version, it says here: "He can requisition some without the proper papers." Now I'll just leave it at that and I'll keep it for further arguments. The other question I have for you, sir, is that in your handwritten version, I take it says that there is none, like to say there is no fuel. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm uncertain as to whether my learned colleague is asking the witness to point out discrepancies in the translation. I assume that that's the basis of it. I think that's a perfectly appropriate thing to do, but the fact is that there are discrepancies in the translation, as the witness has already testified to, and I don't know that the witness is in a position to vouch for the accuracy of the translation of the documents he prepared in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the process was it went from something that is listened to on a tape that is put into a notebook, that then goes into a typed version, and then that it goes to a translation. Now, we have two translations. A translation of the notebook and we have a translation of the typed version. And they're different. So I just want to make sure that I can correct with the witness, he can tell us what he wrote down simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have, as you may have noticed, discussed this in a couple of seconds. We do agree that you should proceed along the same lines that you have been doing, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll keep it as short as I can, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So my question, sir, was simply: Does your handwritten version say that there is none, in terms of that there is no fuel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: My version says: "They have problems with fuel, there isn't any."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So again, Mr. President I just note that the next document the translation that we have of the typed version says that they don't have enough and not that there is no fuel, and I will move on to my next question which has to do with tab number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. I think I can anticipate what Mr. Vanderpuye is going to say. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the issue is, if my colleague wants to put the question to the witness, is to ask the witness to compare what's in his notebook with what's in the printout since these are the subject of independent translations, and if there is a discrepancy between what's in the notebook and what's in the printout then that perhaps would be more enlightening than asking the witness to compare what's in his notebook with what's in a translation of another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could just add a little background to this, it may be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- and I may have said this before but we have many times just translated -- because the printouts and the notebooks are so close, many times there is only one translation. Sometimes there are two. And CLSS is doing this and they don't always match and so we have always provided the Defence with all versions of translations, just so to be on the safe side. But that's where the problem is. We are trying to reduce that problem, and we appreciate the Defence, especially those that speak the language, to identify those things for us. But that's the problem we are having. And as this all these things get closer to a final product, we hope to reduce those translation differences because it's just -- it's just natural that there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. But on the same score, wouldn't the information that the witness can provide be equally helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think Mr. Bourgon's questions in that regard have been helpful and I don't think we have a real problem with that as long as we keep the translations, the CLSS translations, to what they are. So I don't think we have a problem with Mr. Bourgon's approach on this in -- a particular problem, but it's easily turned into a CLSS issue to make it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, as you can imagine, to the Trial Chamber, particularly when facing or confronting a witness with a document that allegedly is attributed to him, that would be the document that you should be addressing yourself to primarily. Of course, it is of paramount importance that we are not left in the dark if the -- any of the parties, I mean it's not just the Defence teams but also the Prosecution, if you feel that there is a shortcoming in any other document we may have available, which purports to be a translation of the document that you are referring to. I mean, so you can, of course, ask the witness to at least confirm to us what he has allegedly written in that notebook because that would make us, put us in a position where we can then see whether there is some valid arguments which relates to the translations that we have been provided with. Which I am sure, if that would be the case, it's a matter that will be attended to in due course. But I think the way you have been proceeding is correct, but do always also please keep in mind that the notebook is the fundamental document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I also acknowledge with my colleague the suggestion of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Just on the point that's been raised by the Prosecution, Mr. Bourgon, it would be helpful to me to hear the witness's comments on the typed version, with reference to his handwritten version, because that will be a comparison in the same -- in the two languages -- in the same language. So it would be helpful for me to at least to have that comment which is different from the translation issue. It's whether the notebook varies from what was typed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically we have two issues that possibly and preferably you would address. One if it's -- the witness can himself offer us some kind of evaluation on a comparative analysis basis between the two documents that Judge Prost has referred to, and then of course, the questions of translation, if they at least exist in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In this case, I don't think that the problem is one of translation. I just think it's two different translations. And I like the suggestion, Your Honour, about the fact of looking at the typed version. I did not think that I had the exact typed version of the translation I was referring to, but I see that I do have it, and that is on 1105 D, for Delta, and I have the exact one which was translated. So if I can have this one on the ELMO, 1105 Delta. Sorry, I said ELMO again but I meant e-court -- or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, this conversation is towards the bottom of the document, at 9.22, if we can scroll down, 1105 Delta, and go -- yes, the one that is just at 9.22 where it says "Krsmanovic." Now, we have both -- can you read this specific typed version and let me know whether it matches what was in your notebook? Maybe you could read it out loud so that the interpreters can give us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That -- just sorry to interrupt, that adds a new intercept to the match so it's -- unless they have a -- unless they have one that they can read to then we are going to get a third version of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. Let's proceed with the way suggested by Mr. Bourgon. If then we get into a fix, obviously we will find some kind of a solution, but for the time being, I think it's perfectly okay to go, to proceed the same way. Have a look, please,. Did you understand the question from Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can just, sir, just read, please, the paragraph that is in the middle of your screen right now, which is a typed version. If you can read this out loud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: "Conversation between unidentified participant X with Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. X tells him that he has only two buses. They cannot requisition some without papers." I cannot see all the way until the end but in the next line it says: "Order. They have problems with fuel. They do not have enough."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I've already asked you the differences and I will stop here, Mr. President, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out maybe for the benefit of the court at least on the screen in front of me there is a word that's cut off from the right side of the document in relation to this particular intercept, and I don't know whether or not the witness can see it or that was part of what he read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know because I can't see what the witness can see but -- it's on the ELMO, okay. All right. So I just want to confirm one thing. One previous question that was put to you, sir, by Mr. Bourgon was what you had precisely jotted down in the notebook, and in answering that question, you had stated in relation to fuel: "They have problems with fuel, there isn't any." This is what you had answered. Now, going through the transcript as we have it, instead of the words "there isn't any" or there is none," at least the interpretation that we have is "they do not have enough." Is that what appears in this document that you have next to you, or does it actually say the same thing as you stated earlier? Because the two things are not exactly -- not exactly, they aren't the same. There isn't enough is not tantamount to saying there isn't any. So ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree absolutely. The end of these two versions is different. In my version, in the original version, it says, clearly, "They have problems with fuel. There is none." While the typed version, the version that is not mine, and which I did not see, it says, "They have problems with fuel. There isn't enough." I don't know why this is so. Again, I note that I had no access to the typed version, and this was done by someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I think we have cleared that in a definitive manner, I suppose, and you can proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've highlighted in what my view were three differences between the two, and those will be the object of arguments later on. For now I'd like to move to tab number 9, and that is Exhibit 1147. And I would like, if possible, to have both Alpha and Bravo on the e-court, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 1141, maybe. Yes, it's a 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you see the conversation where it's at 1141 -- not there yet, okay. That's the English version. And Bravo is 1553, that's the handwritten, that's Charlie. If you look at 1553 -- it's not there. Yes, the one on the right, which begins with Milanovic. Do you see the typed version on the right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is simply: Is that one of those conversations or intercepts that you transcribed as a summary of a longer conversation and in which you only kept the essential part but there is nothing verbatim in that intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
