utterances.text: I would like to ask you, if possible, to show me the handwritten intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Handwritten is 1141 C or Charlie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's my last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not foreclosing on any one of you. I mean, this is why basically we had agreed in the first place that all these witnesses should come and be available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true, it's a summary probably of a longer intercept, a summary with information that was important to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's important that this is not being shown on the monitors. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my last question to you, sir, simply this type of summary, to use your word probably of a longer intercept, was that a procedure that was used only by you or by the others also? And was that part of the verbal protocol that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you that specifically. I know that I did it. I assume, I cannot remember, specifically that others did that too. We sometimes had intercepts or conversations that went on for half an hour. For example, many of them knew each other, so they exchanged a lot of private, personal information that was not important to us. They would then just process the parts that were important for us. There was no need because of all the problems we had with tapes, notebooks and so on, to transcribe everything. So at least I, but we, would usually just make a summary of things that were of importance for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I will just end then with one question, simply that if I considered these intercepts and procedures that you were following, would you agree with me that if I want to have something that I can really rely on today, it would be for me -- the proper route would be to have those tapes and to listen to those tapes myself? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's your objection, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would object to it because first it's framed in terms of a hypothetical, and the question actually presumes an answer that I think is uncalled for under the circumstances. The witness doesn't have the capacity to know what would be reliable to my esteemed colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see any validity in your objection, Mr. Vanderpuye. It's a question he can safely answer. Knowing especially now that he has seen the various documents, whether he would agree with the proposition made to him by Mr. Bourgon. So please go ahead and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the laws, but I know one thing: What I have written is correct. We didn't compile this material for the purposes of this institution where we are right now. This was material that was interesting to us. It's material once it was typed and once it was sent out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think this is beyond what you actually asked him, Mr. Bourgon. The question that was put to you was the following: If one were to consider these intercepts and procedure that you were following, would you agree with us that if we really wanted to have something that we can really rely to then, then the best thing to have would be the tapes themselves. Would you agree to that proposition? He can tell us yes or no and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank. Who is next? Mr. Stojanovic, we will have a break at 12.30, how long do you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are counting on 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Since you already have this intercept before you, let us continue where you left it off with Mr. Bourgon. Would you please read this conversation, the sentence beginning with the words "following that" or "after that"? Would you please read out from your handwritten text, the rest of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: "After that, he asks from the person on duty, Zlatar, Lieutenant-Colonel Blagojevic, a typist."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have the text in front of you, the transcribed text, typed text. Would you please read what it says there, after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: "After that, from Zlatar on duty, Lieutenant-Colonel Blagojevic, a typist. Colonel Vikic will come to fetch her."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the typewritten text doesn't reflect in its entirety the handwritten text and that the word in B/C/S, "trazi" is missing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What would "trazi" mean? Because to us, knowing that it is missing, is one piece of information, but it's not all the information that we would require. What does "trazi" mean? If the interpreters can help me. "Trazi." Looking for? Okay. Looking for. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Requests, looking for, seeks, anything of that, depending on the context. But the sentence is extremely ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, did you receive the translation and may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The translation that we received, and I can state it, is that the interpreters consider the line to be ambiguous and it means requests, looking for, seeks, anything of that, depending on the context but the sentence is extremely ambiguous. This is what we have. This is why I asked what is the meaning of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your leave, I will continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to simplify this, can we agree that the text that you wrote does not fully correspond to the typewritten text in this portion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at another discrepancy. The sentence beginning with the words "they are not there, his warrant officer replied." Will you then please read what you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: "Loader or bulldozer."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So we will agree, won't we, that the first word is "loader"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at the typewritten text. Will you please read out what it says there, after the word "requests." What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: It says "backhoe excavator or bulldozer."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that a loader and a backhoe excavator are not identical pieces of machinery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: In principle, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that there is a discrepancy here as well, a discrepancy between what you heard and wrote down in your own hand and what was typed here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes. What was typed here by somebody else. I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in Paket communication, to your superior command, you sent the typewritten text, it was either typewritten or computer processed, so that was the version that was sent, not your handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that in the previous example, the superior command received the version containing the words "there isn't enough" rather than "there isn't any"? And that this information is quite different from what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes. It's different from what I heard and wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know of any additional problems of this nature, when the typewritten text did not fully correspond to what you heard, transcribed and wrote down in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that at all until I came here and received documents to that effect here. I have already said several times that I had no control, in fact I had no insight, into the work of the typist who typed these texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have just a few more things to ask you now. You were there working as an officer practically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes. One could say so, although the relationships that existed there were quite different. It was mostly of a friendly nature. That was the kind of relationship that existed between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a military rank at the time, in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't think so. Or perhaps I did. Perhaps I was a corporal but I'm not sure. I really am not positive as to what I was at that time. A sergeant perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to your workplace, I don't want to mention the name of that location, I don't want to go into private session, was it your task to organise the work and to supervise the members of your squad, or were you also someone who, as a rule, worked in shifts and listened to conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: In addition to some other duties, I always, as a rule, worked. Well, it's difficult to say as a rule. But at least in 80 per cent of the cases, I also worked in shifts. They counted on me as one of the persons working in a shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that doesn't mean that you were there to replace somebody, but as a rule you were scheduled to work in certain shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that as you listened to intercepts, you began to recognise voices, timbre of voices and other features of people who you listened to in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make any notes about that, about features of certain voices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you are not aware of any records that were kept recording certain features of persons that you were listening to, that there were no such archives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: In the group that was under my supervision, we had no such records. Now, as to other groups, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you listened to these intercepts, did you recognise those who were in those conversations and do you remember who those people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult for me to tell you. It's been quite a long time. And I don't even remember the real names of the people that I worked with at the time because as I said, many years have passed and I saw those people only then and never since. At least some of them. At the time when we were doing this work and listening to intercepts on a daily basis, it was very easy to recognise voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you served in the army, you had training for a signalsman, and you were trained to work on a teleprinter; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the concept and the term of "operations masking"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your superiors ever caution you to pay attention to this false representation and names of people participating in conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at an exhibit. We will need to see it in e-court. Could we please see tab 10 which is OTP Exhibit P01149, 65 ter list -- could we please see the following numbers, 1149C? 1149C on the 65 ter list, thank you. That's the text I'm interested in. Could we see the English version as well so that we can all follow in the courtroom, and this will be my last question. Thank you. Witness, we had occasion to see this intercept; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the upper corner, at the time when you listened to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we see the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Not in this portion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what date it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Not right now, but if I were to see the notebook from which this was extracted, it would be very easy for me to specify the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing this. I don't think it will be contentious, I just wanted to clarify the context. Now, would you please look in the middle section of this intercept, the following sentence, where it says: "D. Do you want me to come there to Cerska from where you are calling?" Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us where Cerska is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Cerska, I think that it is in Podrinje canton. I myself never visited that place, either before or after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please specify in greater detail, because there are many people here who do not know what territory is covered by Podrinje canton. Would I be correct in saying that it's correct -- close to Zvornik, Milici and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes, that would be right. This is all in the general Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why am I asking you this? I would like to know how you interpret this conversation now. Who is D, I suppose that D stands for Deronjic, is addressing when he says, "Do you want me to come down there to Cerska?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: You probably read this entire intercept. When we read it in its entirety, we see that there is an unknown participant in the conversation, who is a mediator or intermediary between Karadzic and Deronjic, and his code-name is Badem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, who is located in Cerska at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I can't know that. Just a minute. Let me read this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do have a little bit of a problem here understanding properly. B in the notebook, the letter capital B, is only shown once there in the third line from the top. Or -- and then subsequently two lines later. You saying that B stands for Badem. On what -- yeah, yeah. And I see that on the top. But on what basis do you come to that conclusion? In other words, what is there in the transcript itself that indicates that there was one person in this conversation that was calling himself Badem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Badem is one of the secret codes. When the call is made, it is made between two switch boards, and two secret names. When I started intercepting this conversation, you can see that I didn't start from the very beginning. Once I started intercepting it, I heard one of the participants introducing himself as Badem and I didn't know how the other participant introduced himself. This is why we have this letter B at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, yes, okay. I accept that, and I understand that, and that is the reason why we don't have the word "Badem" in the -- appearing in the transcript that you made on that day, because it's something that occurred before you started jotting down on the notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason -- if you look at this page on the notebook, you don't see the word "Badem" except at the top near the time and the frequency, and then you have B equals Badem. Right? But the reason why we don't see that word again anywhere on that page is that you had heard the word "Badem" or one of them describing himself as Badem, before you started jotting down the transcript on your notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, Badem is mentioned in the following ones. For example, it says: "B, Badem, yes." And then he says: "Hello, Deronjic, we have contact." And then following that, Badem became the person talking to Badem. That is to say, Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other question. Thank you. But I was referring to what we have on the screen now. Is there a reason why the top line next to the channel and the time of the transcript, in addition to B, Badem, there isn't an indication of D being Deronjic and another person who is supposed to be the interlocutor or intermediary? Why is there only a reference to B, Badem, and not also to D, and possibly an X or a Y or a Z?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, unidentified speaker is marked either with a dash or a letter X. That's how we did it. And in fact we didn't even reflect those who were unidentified. We only marked those who were identified, whose identities we knew. The other ones who were unidentified remained as X or epsilon or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I think I'll cut it short here. But the question was if you had identified Deronjic, why didn't you put, insert his name, on the top line, the first line, where you're indicating who the persons taking part in the conversations are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, based on this conversation, Deronjic was calling from the secret code Badem, and later on, when he started speaking, I simply transformed that secret code into his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those were precisely my questions. And I would simply like to ask the witness to reply to my earlier question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that as you read this text, one of the participants, Karadzic, intermediary, Badem, Deronjic, are located in Cerska? Would that be your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Can you please allow me to read it once again? Based on what you said I would agree that you, that unidentified participant in the conversation was located in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is next? Madam Fauveau, I think we can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. That would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can have a break of 25 minutes instead of 30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. How long do you think --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can I ask Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you have the next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do, we have trying to -- we saw that this might happen even though it's a little different than our estimate but we'll try to see if we can catch up with our e-court documents and have him ready to go, or we can bring him tomorrow morning, whatever is -- I have mentioned both options and I think the Defence is fine with him in the morning but obviously we'll do what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will see how long this is going to take and then we'll decide accordingly. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you stated that the frequency was determined by way of an order. Is it fair to say that you would listen to various frequencies through the RR 1 and the various frequencies also through the RR 800?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you're asking, but we were listening to different channels, to different frequencies, depending on the order. In this specific case, for example, when we were working on this problem, we all did that on one frequency and a certain number of channels, on the same frequency.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you would listen to one single frequency on various channels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, depending on the circumstances, you would encounter situations where you had two conversations, consecutive situations, and they were transcribed in the notebook with various answers, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: I don't know that I was able to see that anywhere. It could happen in case there was a conversation with the RRU800 and one with the RRU1, but I would have to see it actually in order to tell you exactly what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1133C?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, these are three conversations, three various conversations, with -- they are consecutive and with no frequency. Can you determine whether they were listened to through RR 1 or through RR 800, simply by looking at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: RRU800.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Because of the channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this mean that RRU1 did not have any channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: At the moment, I cannot remember if the RRU1 had channels. But according to the channels and the direction, you can tell that this was the RRU800.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown P2320, page 106. Sorry, page 36, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this page, there are two different frequencies. They follow one another. Could you tell me whether they are from the same device or from two different devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: These are frequencies from different sets. The first intercept is the RRU800 frequency. And now I can see, I can refresh my recollection, that the second intercept would then be from the RRU1 frequency.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, it could happen that there would be two conversations on two different frequencies and that they would follow one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Yes. Because we had generally one notebook into which we entered the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore fair to say that if the frequency was not noted in the page, that the person typing the document was not able to determine the frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: That is not true. They could establish the frequency that it was -- the work was being done on if they had the channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is there anything in the document that makes a difference between RRU1 and RRU800, apart from the frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: Nothing else. I don't know if you know, but the RRU1 works on a frequency, as far as I can remember, because I haven't been active for a long time, from 190 to about 300 megahertz, and the RRU800 operates on a frequency from 600-something up to 900 megahertz. So based on that, you can establish what was done on the RRU1 and what was done on the RRU800, especially because the RRU800 is already set to channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you therefore mean to say that RRU1 did not have any channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: From what I can see, I think that it did not have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement, you provided in November 1999 to the OTP, you said that -- not you personally but members of your team would write the dates at the -- at the beginning of a day in the notebook. Would you allow for the possibility that dates were not written in every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-140
utterances.text: During my preparations, I saw that the date was not entered every day. However, it should have been entered every day. It doesn't mean that you couldn't establish the date of a given intercept on the basis of previous or subsequent dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there is not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There are no questions, no further questions for you, neither from the Prosecution nor from the Bench, which means that your testimony concludes here. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom very soon, and on behalf of the Tribunal I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and you will be receiving all the assistance you require to assist you in your journey back home. And on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deal with the tendering of documents. Let's start with the Prosecution documents. Has this list been circulated amongst the Defence teams? It has?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe it has, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's try to economise on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I'd like to check both English translations of handwritten note as well as the typed version are tendered as exhibit. Is it the case or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, take a look at 1149. This document says what are tendered is A, B, C, D, with only one English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct. The singular English translation is what we have available at this time. That's not to suggest obviously that other translations or further translations can't be made but that is what we have available to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I remember I saw two interpretations at the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Referring specifically to tab number 9? Number 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is Your Honour referring to the -- I believe that related to number 6, tab number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think they are related to what we have behind tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, tab 6 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And tab 6 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have two English translations of tab 2 -- tab 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. For tab 6 there is only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can put up the curtains again, or do you need them down for the next witness? Usher? We need them down for the next witness. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. There is only one for tab 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay? There are two for tab 9. Is that right? Yes, that's right. Two for tab 9. That's indicated as well, right? And two for tab 7? There is two for tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there, take tab 9. What is tendered is the only translation of printout, not the handwritten note. I'm mistaken. I beg your pardon. They are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, they are on the list. I was just mistaken as to what tab I was referring to. And I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason I was confused is that they are not included in this packet, the physical printout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's actually news to me, and I apologise to the Court. I wasn't aware that they didn't make it into that packet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back to the list. I have only one English, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I suggest we go tab by tab instead of doing the ten tabs together, because for each tab there are different submissions to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start. You have the list. Is there any particular document that -- from that list that the Prosecution seeks to tender that you object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the same reason that was explained by my colleague with the last witness, the handwritten notebook, P02319, 2320, 2321, 2322 and 2323, all of those we have an objection that they -- that these documents would be admitted. Now, as far as the -- for the others, once we go into the various documents going from 1099 until 1149, those are the ten tabs, then I have submissions different for each of those tabs, depending on whether or not there is a translation available or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with the last five, the handwritten notebooks. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would submit that those notebooks go actually to the heart of the witness's testimony, to the extent that the witness indicated that he had actually compared the entries in the notebooks which are originals to the photocopies that are being tendered in tabs 1 through 10. Moreover, I believe he was asked certain questions on cross-examination to which he indicated if he had an opportunity that he could readily verify certain information that was put to him that are actually contained in the notebooks, and so on those grounds, I think they are appropriate for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bourgon, for the record at least, could you, since you've just intimated an objection without indicating the basis for that objection, I know that you referred to the same or identical objection tabled during the testimony of the previous witness, but if you could repeat that for the record, it would help us then reach our decision here and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our objection is as follows. First of all, these documents were never included on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list of proposed exhibits; that is the first thing. The second is that for these five documents, there does not exist a request by the Prosecution to amend its Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. The next reason is that not all of these exhibits have been shown to the witness when he testified. The next reason is that we have the excerpts from those notebooks along with translations and that is enough. Getting the full notebook will only confuse the issue. And finally, if should there be a will by the Trial Chamber to admit these documents, then we would respectfully submit that the complete notebooks have to be translated so that we have side by side the full notebook and the full translation. So for all these five reasons, Mr. President, we say that those five exhibits should not be admitted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to add anything in this regard, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would only point out that to the extent that the Defence has challenged the authenticity, reliability of the intercepted material it seems to me appropriate to establish the reliability or authenticity of that material to the extent that they exist within the notebooks. It would be impossible, frankly, to admit a page or an intercept, an original intercept, from the notebook without admitting the entire notebook, and certainly we are not tendering the notebook with the hopes that the Court would consider every aspect of the notebook unrelated to the given intercept to which it relates. So I'm not entirely clear as to the genesis of my esteemed colleague's objection. I understand it on procedural grounds, and I think it is a relevant objection. I think, however, substantively the Defence has been on notice of the intercepts that were going to be offered or tendered into evidence this case, and there is, for all practical purposes, no substantive difference between the material that is actually in the notebooks from the material that Defence has been on notice of and, as I understand it, for a substantial amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I saw you being tempted to intervene and I'm not quite sure whether you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wish to, although I was trying to study the response. In any event, we concur obviously with my learned colleague from the Defence. But the other important issue is, Your Honour, if the Prosecution gives us 20 exhibits, let's say, and they don't use all 20 with the witness and the Court allows that, it puts the Defence at a disadvantage. Similarly we can add in our exhibit list 50 documents and only use one. And although I'm guessing, but I don't think the Court would allow or the Prosecutor would allow all our exhibits could be entered into evidence, even though we list them in our exhibit list merely because we list them as inadequate. If the Prosecutor wanted to ask specific intercept material or documents of a witness, then he should have walked through that same list he gave us. The Defence should not be given multitude of documents, they don't ask about those documents, we constrain our cross-examination based on that, and we expect to be treated in the same fashion as the Prosecutor is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I see there Mr. McCloskey would like to join in the debate. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just the next witness, my plan was to ask him if the 14 intercepts that he took down whether he recognises the handwriting in the notebooks and maybe a couple of questions and leave it at that. If we go through with every intercept on every notebook, we'll be here forever, and so this particular line of questioning is -- I don't think it's appropriate, nor necessary for me to go through every intercept that every intercept operator has dealt with, whether it's acts or conducts or not. The important thing is that they have the ability to cross-examine on these documents and the witness is present, but especially for 92 ter I really -- and of course we would be very happy to hear the Court's ruling on that because I will adjust my direct testimony, if necessary. But I don't see -- you're going to be hearing lots and lots more information on these intercepts from the people that were actually speaking on them and from documents and other things. So this is -- this is really the idea of going over every intercept is not necessary, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically two things. We'll adopt the same procedure that we adopted on previous occasion. These are being entered and marked for identification purposes. It's also the understanding of the Trial Chamber, and correct us if we are wrong in this understanding, that in seeking the admission of these notebooks, you are not seeking to enter into evidence all the contents of the -- contained in each of these notebooks. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We wanted the Court, as had previous courts, showed an interest in the whole notebook, especially when the witness makes a reference to I need to see the whole notebook to figure out the date. But the other intercepts that we are not talking about, that's not -- we don't need that to have that technically as part of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That corresponds exactly to what we have been thinking, but of course we understand that other witnesses have come or may still come that will be referring to parts of these notebooks, and I think that is understandable. And we'll leave it at that. So, now, I thought we would have simplified this exercise but obviously we are not. Let's start with the first one. P02317. This is the witness's previous statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. Any objection to having this admitted? None? This will be admitted with that number under seal. The pseudonym sheet, which is 2318; again I would imagine no objections there. It's admitted under seal. And then we start with 1099, which would correspond to what we have behind tab 1. So this first set of documents, I understood from what you said earlier, Mr. Bourgon, that you have some objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Concerning this 1099, I have no objections concerning A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I have to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Bravo being the translation of the document Alpha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Or vice versa, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Alpha being the translation of document Bravo. Noting, however, that there is of course some additions that were put in place by CLSS but that would be the object of further representation, if need be, at a later time. With respect to C and D, for those, Mr. President, unless we have translations that are made of these documents, then we do not want these documents admitted on the record unless we have a chance to see a translation of exactly what is in the typed version, and we have two different typed versions, and that's for the reasons that we during the cross-examination that we highlighted the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I understand -- as I understand you, as regards A and B there is no objection. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please be brief because we have got very limited time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that A is a translation of B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is when are we to expect the translations of C and D, because usually we would mark these documents for identification purposes only and they would be upgraded to full documents once this has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Well, we will undertake to do that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, because I think Mr. McCloskey has got some other ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I'm sorry, Mr. Vanderpuye. In dealing with these intercepts over the years with CLSS, getting translations for everything has not been possible. We can attempt that. It's a very long and tedious process. The danger we face is that instead of using the -- one of the originals, they get a whole different translation and we get a third translation that isn't related to the others. If we were very careful and we make sure they have the previous one, then it helps. But in many cases it's only the difference in a word or two, or three words, and we can attempt to do that and we are trying to identify those intercepts where there are differences so that is clear, because as we saw it was important, we had no gas on one and enough on another. And those sorts of things we want, of course, everyone in the court to be aware of. And we can attempt to get translations for everything but that will be a long process, and we are trying to at least identify the key issues. Like this in the cross-examination actually helps us identify what is of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But still, if you seek, according to me, at least, I speak for myself, but if you seek to tender C and D, which are in B/C/S, the Defence teams have -- and plus the accused, have every right to have them translated into one or more of the official languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's our view that they are, that the translation is in most of the cases identical or practically identical. I can try to turn the Tribunal into an identical 100 per cent situation. It's just practically difficult. And as I mentioned, when you give a translation it comes back with other things that aren't really different. For example, we did this on one intercept that we wanted to clarify it on, and the original intercept had cowboys and that came back as livestock drivers. And this kind of problems will create more issues than help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, again, please as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. We are not talking about translating the same documents. Cross-examination has shown that the documents are different; therefore, they each require their own translation. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are perfectly correct. So our position is as follows: If you have no intention to translate C and D, then I think the only option that you have is not to seek to tender those two documents and restrict yourself in relation to tab 1 to A and B. Otherwise, if you continue to seek their admission they need to be translated, as they are, and for that reason, A and B are being admitted. C and D are temporarily at least marked for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On this, Judge Kwon has come up with a brilliant suggestion that I think in the spirit of cooperation that has been prevailing throughout, since we started this trial, if in relation to these untranslated documents you feel that they don't need to be translated because there is no significant difference between what has already been translated, then please do come forward and communicate this to the Prosecution so that we will try to avoid unnecessary translations. However, where you request the translations, it must become -- it must be considered as a sine qua non. All right. Yes, next set, 1100. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The same applies, Mr. President. A is a translation of B, and we have no problems with that. But C and D require their own translations. Now, that being said, I note that both C and D have identical text, and for this purpose only one of the two needs to be translated. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one? No, which one doesn't need to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Either C or D. Because they are the same text. As long as we have the translation of the same text, then we have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So A and B are admitted. The rest are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being reminded that basically we have agreed that since the question of admissibility of intercepts in general is going to be dealt with in due course, that we are admitting intercepts on that caveat, that they are being marked for identification, but the difference will be -- the reason would be different. Okay. Madam Registrar, in order to economise on time, what's in bold lettering, bold characters will be under seal, all right? Okay. As regards 1102.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are no problems with A, B, C and D. A being a translation of B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: C being a translation of D. However, once we get into Echo, Foxtrot, and Golf, E, F, G, then there are no translations, and I did not have the time at this point to see if they are three of the same or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the same position, all marked for identification. Last three, of course, in addition pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to that particular exhibit, it does occur to me that actually all three of them are textually identical. And in that case, would it satisfy the Defence if one of the three is translated as opposed to all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Try to deal with that once the sitting is over. Let's try to go through this as quickly as we can. 1103. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is no problem with A, which is a translation of B; so A and B is okay. And then when we move to C and D, it's also the same thing, so C and D is the same. And then once we get into E for Echo, this one requires a translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So same position as before. 1103E in addition would require translation before it is admitted. Yes, 1105.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This one has -- so A is a translation, it's not possible to tell which one, if A is in fact a translation of B. Because of the number at the end, we cannot see the number at the bottom, which is 0006, and that doesn't match the numbers for the other documents. So for this one, we don't know what A is a translation of what, just looking at the number at the bottom of the document. So this one has to be sorted out completely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't we do one thing because we are running short of time in any case. Could we invite you to go deeper, somewhat deeper, in the examination of all these documents and agree amongst yourselves what needs to be translated and that what doesn't need a translation, come back to us tomorrow morning, and we'll take it up from where we are leaving it today. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Agreed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, I think we can postpone also tendering of any Defence documents. I doubt if there are any but I suppose aren't. So we can stop here for today. Tomorrow we'll start with a new witness and also finish the tendering process related to this witness we finished today. Thank you so much. Mr. Bourgon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, there was Prosecution Exhibit 1467 and 1468, the two maps. I don't know if you have them on your list, but these were not shown to the witness or used. They do have a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my list is not updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's probably on the list of exhibits but not on the list to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My mistake, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Have a nice afternoon and see you tomorrow morning.
